Yeah. I was able to play my piece, which you may or maybe heard last night, Dear Ruth, written in dedication to my mother with uh the Lincoln Center Jazz Orchestra, and uh I'm very proud to uh …
Did you orchestrate it?

Yes. I did. Yeah. And uh, and uh it was uh, at the last minute as I was walkin' – of course we rehearsed, but at rehearsal I was gettin' lost, you know, uh, my uh, my chords were overshadowed by the orchestra. So I said, "What can I do?" I mean I was in an unconscious dilemma and then on the way to the piano at the performance, after I made my little speech, I had to go back to Ellington. You play it way up high in octaves and it cut right through. So I was very proud of that decision, a last minute uh decision. Reminds me of the invasion of Normandy … No, I'm only kidding. [chuckles] Nothin' to do with that. But uh, that was a uh uh uh, a bright moment in my uh memory uh, recent memory. It was quite an occasion. Yousef Lateef was brilliant uh, everybody else, too, that I, I tried to remember some of the other recipients uh, um, Bill Holman uh, uh Annie Ross – she did a beautiful song – and uh, Kenny Barron. He elected to play a solo. He played, just played a beautiful original piece uh by himself. So uh …
Muhal.

Oh yeah, Muhal. He came … well, see, they uh did it uh alphabetically so Muhal was first, and he had a very exciting, innovative piece. Oh man, it was dramatic because it was uh … you could see Wynton kind of uh chuckle he would cause because his approach was totally uh, uh different from most conductors, you know. He, he was, he started the piece and then he walked off stage lookin' at his watch as if he was gonna time uh how long they would play in his absence, which was a few minutes. And he came back. Well, he started first on the piano by himself. Then he got up and he started and then he walked off, you know, like he was marching [chuckles] for the watch. It was, it was incredible. And uh, so uh, that was a nice … All my family was there uh, all my offspring and everything. In fact uh I was uh announcing a … I was introducing people who had met my family. I said, "This is the uh cast to uh All in the Family … All My Children, I beg your pardon. You, you'll excuse me [chuckles]. So uh, it was a bunch of us there uh … My granddaughter, she's the only New York resident, the rest of them live places like North Carolina, Philadelphia and uh St. Louis.
You mentioned your family, obviously your mother has been a persistent thread … You played the piece last night, it’s on the 2009 album. Uh but, you haven't introduced us to your immediate family.
Right.
So, why don't you do that.

Well, uh my first marriage was uh back in the days when I was with uh J.J. Johnson in the uh '60s, I think it was. Yeah, '60s. When I was with Art Blakey and … and that marriage uh uh produced uh three children – two boys and a girl. The two boys were born uh just about two years apart, very close, you know. Uh, not quite two years, but say uh, a year and eleven months apart. So uh, when one of 'em's birthday changed, they are the same age for one month and then it changes, you know. So, then the girl, her name is … Uh, their names are Carl and uh Rodney Walton. And uh both named for friends I had encountered in my youth along the way, and I just picked 'em out. I, I was uh not very patient with pickin' out names. I just tried to think of somebody I'd known and uh, so uh, I still have no regrets. Their names slowly became them, you know, fit them. And my daughter's name was Cedra which is a, I guess you could say uh some kind of … It's not an anonym. What do you call that? Acronym? When you uh combine, instead of C-E-D-A-R, she's C-E-D-R-A, Cedra Walton. And uh, then about another union, you … last but not least, uh, her name is Nyesha Walton and uh, that's a combination of Naima, which was John Coltran's wife and Iesha which was uh McCoy Tyner’s wife at one time. So I can see the name of Nyesha. But now there's hundreds of Nyeshas I see, read about in different uh instances uh situations. So uh, and uh, I just always felt that uh in the days when I was mostly a sideman and uh, uh, you could say strugglin', to a degree, with this not-so-small family, um, I managed to raise uh, raise them quite uh … none of them have ever been arrested, [chuckles] you know. That's one way to look at it, of course, uh, and uh, uh, two of 'em uh graduated uh, uh college uh now, the granddaughter now has graduated college, so I'm, I'm proud of that. And uh, the uh …they are gainfully employed uh, so uh, I'm uh, very proud because I always had this thing runnin' through my head that you can't raise a family and be a jazz musician. Not in New York. Forget about it. Something's gonna go wrong, but it didn't. I just kept right on … I know there were times, I remember my sons saying uh, "Naw, I don't think I want to be a jazz musician," because we weren't doin' that well. We weren't … we were eating but we weren't uh living luxuriously, you know, so to speak, by comparison. But now, they, they're, they are uh uh among my uh biggest supporters, you know. They were very proud to uh, be uh present at this ceremony. And I was proud too for them to be there.
Have you made provisions, or, or how does your um, this body of work that you've created, that will continue to earn money? In perpetuity.
Right.
As you say.

Well uh, we uh, in my uh current wife, who did not uh, was not the mother of any of these uh offspring I'm tellin' you about, uh we, we are uh, her cousin is a great uh lawyer that does wills, so we're tryin' to figure that out as we speak. But that has not resolved yet, to answer your question directly and uh somewhat bluntly. We haven't worked that out. But uh, that question almost answers itself. Upon my uh demise uh, everything has … is, is to continue and uh, uh, I'll be gone so it'll work out, it'll work itself out. I just hope there's not … It's not enough, I don't think, for anybody to fight over, but you never know. I saw uh an instance uh, the late John Hicks uh, his family, uh, uh, I didn't even know John had been born in Atlanta. I thought he was from St. Louis; that's where I met him, but he was a preacher's son and so he moved around and his father, his last church was in uh in New York. And so uh, and then I noticed a lot of his

family members uh had come up from, I think, Atlanta, and there was uh, uh dissension among his family about … They had thought that he had uh, uh gleaned uh considerable amount of revenue from his work, but uh, uh I don't think there was enough to around, but I don't know why, though, because I wasn't … John was always doin' some… He was a terrific pianist. That's uh what I'd rather say about him. But on that subject, I did see some uh uh uh, there was some alleged bickering about the uh, uh, the uh, the uh, estate. And uh, I don't know how that's going now because this was a couple of years ago. But uh, there could be some bickering, but uh I, I'm uh, uh, uh in the process now of uh getting a will and uh that will stipulate where everything goes, if there's uh, uh, you know, a … presuming there will be something [chuckles] you know, to go out to everybody.

You, you uh, you know, soloists, trios, sextets … and now with your award, quartets and all these small group configurations, are we going to see Cedar Walton orchestrate his compositions for larger presentations? Is that something that you would see doing?

Uh, yes, but not that anxiously. I like the small group concept, context. I'm more comfortable with that. But uh, John Faddis was uh good enough to invite me out to uh the Chicago School of Music where he uh presides and has an orchestra, and what we did was … Dear Ruth was the only one I orchestrated. But uh Frank Foster had a marvelous uh orchestration of uh Firm Roots that uh we borrowed, we were able to rent them from, you know, and Rufus Reid had about three uh we used, and uh, it seems like there was somebody else who … Oh yeah, there was a guy in the, in the Air Force uh that had uh produced a wonderful arrangement of Bolivia that uh the Monday Night Orchestra has in their book uh at the Vanguard, uh-hm. And their version was thrilling, so we had enough material but I didn't orchestrate it all. I just orchestrated Dear Ruth … 'cause orchestration uh is uh something I do uh when uh, if there's a paycheck over there – I hate to admit this uh, America [chuckles] – I'll write and then pick up the check. So, back to capitalism. I like the small group. I really do. I'm not hiding from the orchestra, I just [chuckles] uh, I'm not avoiding uh uh uh the big uh the big band. Some people can do it all uh, she-knows, uh, uh, uh, Roy Hargrove, he has a big band. Uh, uh there's another big young trumpet player from New Orleans. Uh …
Irvin? Mayfield?
No, trumpet.
Wynton?
No, no, no.
Robert Mayfield has an orchestra.

Yeah … no. But oh, there's one more, and I never forget his name. Uh he's a kind of a chubby guy. He plays terrific trumpet and uh … But he has an orchestra too. Uh, uh, oh man, this is embarrassing because I know this guy so well, and I always make myself remember him … by … 'cause the syllable of his last name, one of the syllables of his last name, but uh … Female Voice: [inaudible]
Huh? Female Voice: I can't think of it either. [inaudible-overlapping voices]
Yeah, you know who I'm talkin' about. He's got a round face … Female Voice: I worked with him.
Yeah. Female Voice: He worked with Alan.....
From New Orleans? Female Voice: Yeah
Yeah. [inaudible-overlapping voices]. His father plays bass. [inaudible-overlapping voices].
Oh, Nicholas Payton.

Yeah. Nicholas Payton. That's an example of … Oh man, I heard his big band. It was terrific. But uh I didn't go in that direction yet but uh, don't give up on me. I might, I might go into that, uh, it's something I, I really enjoy doing and especially at this stage where you, you, you put uh, it's easy to do uh now for me than it was earlier.
I’ll give you the title.
The title of what? The band?
The album.
Oh, you thinkin' about recording. I thought you meant a career in uh big band uh performance.
I mean, you gotta, you know, that’s another paycheck. You must know every producer …
[chuckles]
… and then you know, for every composition, you'll get somethin' …
[chuckles] Yeah.
… the arranger will get somethin' …
[chuckles] No … no …
… you know, it's not back in Columbia days so it would be more.
No, no, it won't be more. It'd be less. In fact that doesn't exist anymore.
Why do’t you call it “Wow”.
W-O … W?
[inaudible-overlapping voices] That’s your favorite word, Wow!
Oh, oh, okay.
...called Wow!
All right.
Pop art [inaudible].
All right.
Wow!
Okay, well uh … I'll uh …
Call it WOW!

[chuckles] I'll uh send the uh, uh … back off from your enthusiasm because I can't compare with that. [chuckles] But uh, thanks for the, thanks for the suggestion. I'll uh, uh duly note it because I, that would be, that would really be a good step forward for me, you know. 'Cause it seems like I, I've, uh I'm, I have so much material for this size group you heard. Uh, it, it's time to make a move if I'm gonna move, maybe expand these pieces and uh see what I could do with that. But of course that would take me away from my booking, you know. I might have to give somebody a commission. [laughs]
[laughs]
So …
[Get?] software.
Yeah. [chuckles]
Get software to do it.
Yeah.
I'll find you some software.
Oh, I appreciate that. Yeah.
It would actually be more efficient because you'll have more time … You'd be like, Oh, I can still make that money …
Yeah.
… and I can go over here and make some more money.
Well, I … [laughs] I love … [inaudible-overlapping voices]
More surprises.

I love the way that you uh envision income from this uh, uh, uh, uh, this form of art, you know. [chuckles] To listen to you, there's a lot of it, you know. You enlarged, you've taken what I've said and multiplied it by 200 or something. And uh, I don't want you uh to uh disillusion whoever investigates this tape that there's a lot of money involved [chuckles] in this, in this enterprise. It's uh, it's just enough, you know, for the city. [laughs] [general laughter]
That's all it has to be.
Yeah. [chuckles] Brower & Female Voice: [inaudible-overlapping voices]
'Cause you can't take it with you.
No, man, uh in the words of Art Blakey, he never saw a Brinks truck follow your hearse. [laughs]
Just ask the Pharoah.
[laughs]
You took ['em, didn't you?]?
Oh yeah, I suppose he did uh …
But [inaudible] …
You think it was Euros or American currency?
No, it was something that preceded all of that..
Probably, yeah, probably bricks. [chuckles] Right in [there?] with Brinks. But uh, yes, that's a good suggestion. I, I'll make a …
It's sort of like what's left for you?
Oh yeah. Well …
What you do is sufficient unto itself. Obviously, people enjoy [being?] busy.
Yes, especially if you don't do it too much. [inaudible-overlapping voices]
But what else is on your horizon?

Uh, yeah, uh, just uh enough of myself, you know, I'm just uh uh, if I got lucky enough to hand down something, I'm proud to do that but uh I'm quite thrilled that uh somebody as far away as Beirut would want me. But even, even I'm gonna play alone, I'm not takin' this group, mind you. Just gonna go there and play it alone uh, two one-hour sets, three nights and uh I, I can't wait to … Those kind of challenges uh excite me. I say, "What the hell am I gonna do?" I mean, I gotta sit down and I gotta play, but uh, who are these … What kind of people are the Lebanese people? Uh …
It's very cosmopolitan.
So yeah, I saw a [C?] on the uh …
It's like Paris.
Yeah, the computer showed me that, the way it looks.
Except bombed out [inaudible].

Yeah. Well uh, we'll have to see can I survive that uh. Very often I miss the bombings by one day. I was in uh Israel and uh we landed in Tel Aviv, and uh we uh went uh to Jerusalem to play in a big library. This was a trio. And uh the uh promoter was a piano player so I was lucky. He, he liked me. And so, and then we went back and when we left Jerusalem, the next day we read about a bombing, and then we played in Tel Aviv that next night in a big hall and it was magnificent. And we flew back to America and on the newspaper, bombing in Tel Aviv. So we, I have uh, uh, uh a reputation, so to speak, of missing them by one day. But of course I didn't stay in that place uh three days like I [will be?] in this one, like I play it like uh like, like the uh, the game plan is to stay in this place three whole days, so I'm uh … You'll be the first one I call when I land back on these shores with uh, with a thanks for your reassuring uh, uh and convincing uh warning uh … if there, if there's such a thing as reassuring, convincing …
Just because I’m skittish doesn't mean you have to be.
Oh, okay, well thank you for that uh … I'll take along with me.
I’ll admit it man, I’m a ninny.

Well, okay. All right. Uh perhaps if you could do uh, uh six sets on the piano, you might consider going. [general laughter] So uh, that's uh, that's my next move uh. No, that's right, there's a … a guy conceived of a, a Jazz Masters group consisting of [inaudible] and Cedar Walton, and we did some things in Europe uh, on the, uh, uh festival circuit last summer. And right after the ceremony that I was describin' to you with the piece Dear Ruth, we did uh, uh, a week, uh five days in uh the [Dizzy's? Disney's?] Coca Cola which is in the same building. And then we did the Playboy Jazz Festival I was describin' how that, that uh …
Was Willard Jenkins orchestrating that?
Uh …orchestrating?
Any of the Jazz Masters [inaudible] Jazz Masters?

No, no. A gentleman named uh … Well, this is just two, two of us Masters: Hutcherson and Walton. So uh, a guy named … Actually, Bobby Hutcherson's manager. His name is Maurice Montoya, so yeah, he put that together.
Duet or was …

No … with David and uh uh Bobby's drummer whose name, name uh escapes me right now. Uh … Eddie Marshall. He's a very good drummer. But he's always been in the Bay Area. He's always, he played with Bobby for years. So it's a very compatible group and uh, he's, he's sending us out one more time to uh Philadelphia later on this month uh, on the 9th to be exact. Then I'll be finished with that group, you know, 'cause Bobby, you know, Bobby has a group and I have a group, so that's enough of that. We, we did a lot, you know.
Tommy's [?] All-Star was another …

Yeah, that was an adventure that was good, positive. [Big Harold Land and Higgins and we all had a great time. Curtis Fuller. That was magnificent. So through the years we've come up with combinations that are very pleasant and uh, uh bookable, you know. So, glad to say that we, we, we went to Japan, Europe and so we went a lot of places in this country and outside this country. So uh …
Okay time for parting shots, but you can’t take them at me.
[chuckles] Time for what a shot?
Parting shots.
Oh yeah.
Just a few little [inaudible] time when you can't like talk about the fact that I can't play piano or can't …
Oh, you can't make those comments, okay. And uh, so uh, should I presume that we are at a conclusion?
Uh-hm.
Okay.
Another two minutes and we want to be done by 12:30, so …

Yeah. Well uh, if uh you would uh be interested in uh what I would have to say to uh a student of the music now uh, uh because I do get a lot of questions uh, people uh, in uh uh generations that precede me uh, uh: How should I pursue this or that and uh and uh one basic thing that I say is uh, just keep striving for excellence. And uh, and choose a path and, and, and, and when you do choose a path in life, you're the only one in there. And if you make the mistake of decidin' to change paths, there's people already in that other path. So, you best stay on … It's almost guaranteed that you reach your goal if you start out early enough, if you stay in that one path. That's what I did, so I have to say, I have to believe that. I never varied from my path and so now I can work in D.C. [chuckles] and uh go to Beirut and uh. D.C. is much safer, according to you. [chuckles]
Depends on what part you’re in.
[laughs] So uh …
Probably the same in Beirut.
Yeah. Well …
Depends on where you …
Yeah. And the timing and everything. But uh I consider this a great honor to uh speak uh in behalf … not speaking in behalf of the Smithsonian, am I? No. Who am I speaking in behalf of?
Cedar Anthony Walton.

Oh, okay. Good. So, it gives me great pleasure to speak to the uh archive department. Is that right? Uh of the Smithsonian because it's a very important uh uh uh place in our country that preserves uh things that uh uh the Institute itself uh uh considers valuable and uh uh … uh historic enough uh to uh preserve. So, I'm grateful to be able to speak on my, on behalf in this context. It's been a pleasure meeting with you uh uh, Bill and Ken and uh until we meet again, I don't suppose we'll … That's why you tried to get all in 'cause we'll never have to meet again. Is, was that the point? [laughs]
No.
No? Okay.
No, I, I would hope that we've opened a door that we could continue to walk through.
Oh, to add to this. Oh man.
I would love to.
Oh well listen uh, I'm available. I, I'll be in my office waiting. [laughs] Just like you. I think he's … Ken, did you send me uh an email, you think? I think so. Kimery: I sent a fax.
Oh, a fax, yeah. Yeah. Fax is becoming outdated now. I mean, it's, I think, but uh not to Kimery: Yeah.
That sounds almost German. No? Okay. Sorry. [inaudible-overlapping voices] …
… bunch of money?
Kimery: Yeah, [he] gave the Museum 80 million dollars, so he got his name on the uh letterhead.
Oh, that's not you? Kimery: No, I'm on the bottom there.
Oh. Kimery: I'm also Kenneth.
Oh, okay. Ah, man. I was … [inaudible-overlapping voices] Kimery: … 80 million dollars.

Yeah. How 'bout that? Billy Taylor, Shirley Horn, Elvin Jones, wow. Well, one thing uh they all have in common: We're old. [chuckles] Right? [chuckles] Which uh, you know, so you're givin' us uh recognition uh beside our uh accomplishments uh, uh that include uh, uh, uh, stayin' on the planet. Right? And being able to elaborate on uh, uh, your, uh, uh, uh, achievements and uh non-achievements or half-achievements. Whatever? Right?
Well, it sets the record straight.
Right. Exactly. That's a good way to put it. Kimery: [whatever it might be?]
Uh-huh.
That’s what the first person, interviews are about.

Right. Uh-huh. Well, I've certainly uh found uh this to be a, a surprisingly uh, uh, uh pleasant opportunity for me to uh express myself from the beginning of my uh music uh explorations to the present time. And I think it's very fortunate that I was able, to be able to perform here in uh Washington, D.C. and uh for you to uh be able to witness that too, and we can use that as a point of reference, which is, gives it a new uh, I mean a, a nice uh point of view, vantage point, I think.
[END OF INTERVIEW]

segments.chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
segments.title: Opening of Day One: setup, name and birth year in Dallas
segments.summary: Brower and Walton settle in, Brower gives the date and the Smithsonian framing, and confirms Walton's name and that he was born in Dallas in 1934.

segments.chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
segments.title: Parents, grandmother Louise and mother's piano; Etta James aside
segments.summary: Walton describes a happy home as an only child with his mother and her mother, his mother's abandoned concert ambitions, and a later Etta James record of a song she loved.

segments.chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
segments.title: Mother's training at Wiley College; first hearing Hank Jones
segments.summary: His mother studied music at Wiley College, took him to Jazz at the Philharmonic where he first saw Hank Jones, and he played by ear on records by Louis Jordan and Nat King Cole.

segments.chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
segments.title: Father the Negro county agent, college and segregation's effect
segments.summary: His father, a Prairie View graduate from a Brazos River farm family, worked as Dallas's Negro county agent; Walton recalls visiting farms and a full life on their side of the color line.

segments.chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
segments.title: Mother starts him on Hanon exercises; 'piano' versus 'keyboard'
segments.summary: Seeing his excitement about Hank Jones, his mother made him learn to read and began with Hanon; he recalls first hearing the word keyboard from George Cables.

segments.chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
segments.title: Clashes with his mother and other teachers coming to the house
segments.summary: Walton and his mother loved each other but argued constantly, so she arranged other teachers who came to the home.

segments.chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
segments.title: Teacher Mrs. Marble, Rhapsody in Blue, and the borrowed wing-tips
segments.summary: He studied with a white teacher, Mrs. Marble, who loved Gershwin and met him secretly in a church, and he tells of playing a Dallas concert in his father's too-small shoes.

segments.chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
segments.title: Ear versus reading in jazz; classical-only lessons in the 1940s
segments.summary: Asked about hearing and reading, Walton says both matter, that his mother gave him notation after he began by ear, and that piano lessons then meant classical; he admires great readers like Freddie Hubbard and Joe Henderson.

segments.chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
segments.title: Not a complete reader, he turns to composing; Mosaic and Blakey
segments.summary: Not being a sight-reader pushed him toward composition; he brought Mosaic to the Jazz Messengers, where Art Blakey learned it by pacing the room before sitting down at the drums.

segments.chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
segments.title: Brower's love of Mosaic; hearing it on Symphony Sid's radio show
segments.summary: Brower says Mosaic was one of his first records, and Walton recalls hearing Symphony Sid announce his composition on the radio while driving around Manhattan.

segments.chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
segments.title: Love of standards; Horace Silver pieces and royalty checks
segments.summary: Asked about his standards repertoire, Walton cites Nat King Cole and Ellington, then talks about the royalty income that still trickles in, including a 28 cent check.

segments.chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
segments.title: Harry Fox Agency, the mis-addressed checks and a $74,000 windfall
segments.summary: On Herbie Hancock's advice he joined Harry Fox; a wrong zip digit held up ten years of checks, which with his mother's estate left him carrying a quarter of a million dollars.

segments.chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
segments.title: How important lyrics are to a jazz musician
segments.summary: Walton says lyrics are very important and cites Lester Young's advice to learn them, admitting he knows only the most important words of each song.

segments.chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
segments.title: Favorite classical composers and the elusive Shostakovich concerto
segments.summary: He worked hardest on Bach, Beethoven, Debussy and Gershwin, loved piano concertos, and describes a Shostakovich orchestral piece heard in a hotel in Austria that he has never been able to identify.

segments.chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
segments.title: Classical taste: Stravinsky, Gershwin, Mozart and Bartok
segments.summary: He recounts hearing The Rite of Spring in college and says he prefers modern composers like Stravinsky and Shostakovich over Mozart, with a liking for Bartok.

segments.chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
segments.title: Beethoven's Moonlight sonata and Hanon as the key training book
segments.summary: He struggled with the second movement of Beethoven's Moonlight sonata and says no other training book mattered as much as Hanon's endless exercises.

segments.chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
segments.title: Learning from George Shearing's simplified books; That Old Feeling
segments.summary: Outside formal study he bought simplified George Shearing arrangements, which gave him That Old Feeling, later his own version on Three Blind Mice with Blakey.

segments.chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
segments.title: Dallas jam sessions with David Newman, Leroy Cooper and older players
segments.summary: As a younger teenager he was invited to jam with David Newman, Leroy Cooper, James Clay and Robert Moss, and played in a joint across from his home with his mother and grandmother Ruth and Louise's permission.

segments.chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
segments.title: James Clay, clarinet by ear and band director J.K. Miller at Lincoln High
segments.summary: He recalls James Clay in the high school band and J.K. Miller letting him play clarinet by ear, mentions studying bass later at Denver, and notes touring Japan with Clay and Fathead Newman as Texas Tenors.

segments.chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
segments.title: Territory bands and Miles Davis asking about J.K. Miller
segments.summary: Walton explains territory bands and tells how at Cafe Bohemia he met Red Garland and Miles Davis, who asked if he knew Walton's high school band director, a former territory musician.

segments.chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
segments.title: Black Dallas music scene: shuffles and no modern jazz
segments.summary: In Dallas only shuffle-style rhythm and blues was played in public, bebop was underground, and the modern players he loved never came through, which made him want to leave.

segments.chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
segments.title: Billy Eckstine's popularity and his Washington connections
segments.summary: Walton talks about Billy Eckstine as a popular singer, his tag on Sophisticated Lady and Ellington calling him William, while Brower lists Washington musicians tied to Eckstine's band.

segments.chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
segments.title: Dallas modern jazz underground; rhythm and blues on the bandstand
segments.summary: Walton says the rhythm was simplified for audiences and everything was rhythm and blues, but at fifteen or sixteen he was glad to be on any bandstand.

segments.chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
segments.title: Race in Dallas: first answer and deferral
segments.summary: Brower asks about the impact of race before Walton leaves Dallas; Walton says it did not exist for him, and they agree to return to it.

segments.chapter: Dillard University and a Columbia Records digression
segments.title: From Dallas to Dillard University in 1951 with Ellis Marsalis
segments.summary: After a mid-term high school graduation his parents shipped him to Dillard in New Orleans, where he enrolled the same day as Ellis Marsalis for about half a semester.

segments.chapter: Dillard University and a Columbia Records digression
segments.title: Dillard campus life: oysters, science teacher, Henry Booker's choir
segments.summary: He had no off-campus music scene in New Orleans, hated the oysters, and remembers joining the a cappella choir under Henry Booker, his first contact with real genius.

segments.chapter: Dillard University and a Columbia Records digression
segments.title: Willie Jones III and the decline of jazz in Los Angeles
segments.summary: Triggered by Dillard memories of Harold Battiste, Walton digresses to the Los Angeles scene, Willie Jones III's rise through Billy Higgins's World Stage, and a Bel Age gig where Willie arrived just in time.

segments.chapter: Dillard University and a Columbia Records digression
segments.title: Self-production, and what record producers actually did
segments.summary: Walton says labels' singles era is fading and he likes to produce himself; he and Brower joke that producers like Orrin Keepnews and Teo Macero mostly asked if you wanted another take.

segments.chapter: Dillard University and a Columbia Records digression
segments.title: George Butler signs him at Columbia; producing Bobby Hutcherson
segments.summary: George Butler signed him to Columbia, where he made Animation and Soundscapes and produced two Bobby Hutcherson albums, enjoying the label's project-number perks.

segments.chapter: Dillard University and a Columbia Records digression
segments.title: Aiming at a bigger audience: turntable hits and orchestrating the tracks
segments.summary: He pitched demo tracks to get signed, wanted a larger audience than a quartet through electric bass, two drummers and ensemble overdubs, and orchestrated around basic tracks on the Hutcherson sessions.

segments.chapter: Dillard University and a Columbia Records digression
segments.title: The money: $7,500 flat plus $1,500 per arrangement
segments.summary: At Brower's prompting Walton reveals Columbia paid $7,500 flat plus $1,500 per arrangement, about nineteen thousand for one project, with continuing publishing royalties.

segments.chapter: Dillard University and a Columbia Records digression
segments.title: Bandmates' reaction: Donald Byrd and Bill Cosby at the Lighthouse
segments.summary: His sidemen did not treat him differently, and Byrd and Cosby teased him at the Lighthouse about the orchestra on his RCA record versus his quartet; Brower and Walton then joke about the Smithsonian archive.

segments.chapter: Dallas memories and the Denver years
segments.title: Ellis Marsalis and multi-instrumentalists in New Orleans
segments.summary: Walton recalls Ellis Marsalis on bass, the New Orleans habit of playing several instruments, and a high-school gig with Harold Battiste; he met James Black and Nat Perrilliat's circle only later or not at all.

segments.chapter: Dallas memories and the Denver years
segments.title: Why he did not return to Dillard and went to Denver
segments.summary: On a family drive to California the Waltons stopped in Denver, and Walton says he perhaps wanted an integrated school and did not go back to Dillard.

segments.chapter: Dallas memories and the Denver years
segments.title: Growing up under segregation: bus signs and fitting rooms
segments.summary: Walton describes taking segregation in stride as a child, the For Colored/For White bus signs and his mother having to use fitting rooms in Fort Worth rather than Dallas.

segments.chapter: Dallas memories and the Denver years
segments.title: Father's last years and his chicken-selling business
segments.summary: He speaks of his father's Alzheimer's, then of the chicken-plucking operation his father ran, Milt Jackson's chicken teasing, and being made to sell eggs and make change.

segments.chapter: Dallas memories and the Denver years
segments.title: His father's discipline: the late car and the neighbor's peaches
segments.summary: Walton recalls his father as stern, with two memorable whippings: coming home a minute late with the car and stealing the Reverend Chambers's peaches.

segments.chapter: Dallas memories and the Denver years
segments.title: Meeting touring stars at neighbors' parties; the autograph book
segments.summary: A neighborhood promoter and the Hills hosted visiting artists like Lena Horne, Billy Eckstine and Marian Anderson, and young Walton collected autographs, living by segregation's two-way rules.

segments.chapter: Dallas memories and the Denver years
segments.title: Dallas blues culture and the Texas tenor label
segments.summary: He says the blues culture was strong but he was too young to go, and that the Texas Tenors phrase came later.

segments.chapter: Dallas memories and the Denver years
segments.title: Choosing the new University of Denver and learning every instrument
segments.summary: Drawn by its newness and supposed co-ed dorms, Walton studied at Denver's Reed Music School, where students played every instrument, which sharpened his orchestration skills.

segments.chapter: Dallas memories and the Denver years
segments.title: No jazz instruction at Denver in the 1950s
segments.summary: Faculty played jazz at night but not in class; Walton and friends did their own little arrangements, none of which entered his repertoire.

segments.chapter: Dallas memories and the Denver years
segments.title: After-hours gigs and Lil's, where touring bands hung out
segments.summary: Playing after-hours gigs led him to skip classes; he describes Lil's, where musicians such as Coltrane, Richie Powell, Hodges and Parker passed through.

segments.chapter: Dallas memories and the Denver years
segments.title: Charlie Parker sits in with his band in Denver
segments.summary: After a Kenton-Gillespie-Parker concert, Parker came to the club and sat in with Walton's band, playing a couple of tunes then dozing off, with Charlie Burrell on bass; Walton places it between 1952 and 1955.

segments.chapter: Dallas memories and the Denver years
segments.title: Denver colleagues and musicians who sat in
segments.summary: Walton says there was little to learn from the Denver players who hired him, such as Shelly Rim and Bob Gray, though visitors like Frank Foster sought him out.

segments.chapter: Dallas memories and the Denver years
segments.title: No first-call in Denver; the Rossonian and Horace Henderson's residency
segments.summary: The Denver scene was too small for a first-call pianist; at the Rossonian he watched Horace Henderson write music fast and sat in when Henderson was away.

segments.title: Meeting Richie Powell and Coltrane; decision to go east
segments.summary: Walton recalls a brief meeting with Coltrane and a night of talk with Richie Powell about Johnny Hodges, showing how Denver gave him access to touring musicians before he drove to New York in 1955.

segments.title: The 1955 drive to Manhattan: gas money, parking and hives
segments.summary: He and a friend arrived with about $75 each, and Walton breaks out in hives from truck fumes and has to park in the Bronx.

segments.title: Musicians urged him to come to New York; his 1947 train trip north
segments.summary: Touring players kept telling him to come to New York, where he had been at thirteen by train; the trains became unsegregated at St. Louis and a Rochester family showed him a different world.

segments.title: First sight of New York and Jackie Robinson at Ebbets Field
segments.summary: On the 1947 trip he was amazed at Grand Central and Brooklyn, saw Jackie Robinson argue with an umpire at Ebbets Field, and he and Brower discuss Robinson's importance.

segments.title: Lunch break and room temperature; scheduling the rest of the interview
segments.summary: The room is overheated, staff arrange for an engineer and lunch, and they work out whether the interview continues tomorrow given Walton's gig and travel.

segments.title: Arriving in 1955 with a friend; abandoning the Manhattan School audition
segments.summary: Walton recalls the YMCA overnight on the drive with a friend named Milton, then planning to enroll at Manhattan School of Music but fleeing the waiting room because he was not ready.

segments.title: First months in New York: Sloan House YMCA, day jobs and his mother
segments.summary: He loved the city, lived at the 34th Street Sloan House YMCA, worked at Macy's and Horn & Hardart, and his mother told him to come home, later hearing him at Carnegie Hall.

segments.title: Early New York circle: Harlem players, Phil Woods and Jackie McLean
segments.summary: He spent the year doing day jobs, practicing on the Y's balcony piano, and playing with obscure Harlem and outer-borough musicians, while Phil Woods and Jackie McLean invited him to sit in.

segments.title: Jam sessions at Connie's in Harlem; Richie Powell again
segments.summary: Walton describes the strong jam-session scene, nightly jamming at Connie's on Seventh Avenue, and seeing Richie Powell there.

segments.title: Drafted: Fort Dix basic training and cavalry wireman duty
segments.summary: He was drafted, went through basic training at Fort Dix, and was a cavalry wireman until Special Services took him; a lieutenant kicked his helmet to wake him.

segments.title: Special Services in Stuttgart, Jazz One and fellow musicians
segments.summary: Walton played in Special Services shows then led the Army band Jazz One in Stuttgart, with Eddie Harris, Leo Wright, Houston Person and Lex Humphries in the orbit.

segments.title: Race in the Army: integrated on paper, separated socially
segments.summary: The Army was formally integrated by 1955-56 but soldiers drank in separate bars, and a show tour was chased out of a redneck bar by thrown bottles.

segments.title: Sitting in with German jazz musicians in Stuttgart
segments.summary: Off-base he sought out German musicians at the Atlantic Bar in Stuttgart, dodging the MPs.

segments.title: Declining to re-enlist and using the Army to shed
segments.summary: He refused officer training because he wanted to return to New York, and used the Army time to practice and write, though none of the music was reused.

segments.title: Back in New York: J.J. Johnson notices him at Birdland's Monday jam session
segments.summary: After discharge in 1958 Walton played Johnny Garry's Birdland Monday sessions, where J.J. Johnson noticed him and soon hired him with Tootie Heath, replacing Flanagan and Elvin Jones.

segments.title: Birdland Monday-night circle: Coltrane's group and the Adderleys
segments.summary: He describes playing a Birdland Monday with a band Coltrane coordinated, opposite the Adderley brothers, and the club blinking the lights on the Adderleys.

segments.title: Touring with J.J. Johnson and his approach to orchestration
segments.summary: The quintet toured in matching uniforms, Johnson featured himself and kept simple sketches, and Walton wonders why Ken Burns left him out.

segments.title: J.J. Johnson versus Curtis Fuller, and J.J.'s absence from Ken Burns
segments.summary: Comparing the two trombonists, Walton says Curtis had a bigger sound and quick ears while J.J. knew more theory; they praise J.J.'s Walkin' and his omission from Ken Burns's series.

segments.title: Joining Benny Golson and Art Farmer's Jazztet for ten dollars more
segments.summary: A ten dollar raise took him and Albert Heath into the Jazztet; Golson wrote everything, which forced Walton back to reading, and Art Blakey then called after remembering him from before the Army.

segments.title: Messengers rehearsal and Blue Note recording routine at Van Gelder's
segments.summary: With Blue Note the band had four days to prepare solos and recorded on the fifth day at Rudy Van Gelder's for minimal fees.

segments.title: The three-horn sound in the Jazztet and Messengers
segments.summary: Brower asks whether a three-horn thread links the Fuller-Jazztet sound and the Messengers; Walton says it was only instrumentation, since Shorter, Golson and he each handled the horns differently.

segments.title: Pianist arranger versus horn-player arranger: Walton, Shorter, Trane
segments.summary: Walton explains that as a pianist he sees notes differently from Wayne Shorter or Coltrane, whose A Moment's Notice orchestration was simple, and mentions Kenny Dorham and Freddie Hubbard's piano skills.

segments.title: Comparing leaders J.J. Johnson, Golson and Blakey; Farmer in the Jazztet
segments.summary: Johnson featured himself, Golson insisted on every note on paper, and Art Farmer happily led the Jazztet voicings and was featured by Golson.

segments.title: Mosaic fails in the Jazztet, succeeds with Blakey's band
segments.summary: The Jazztet needed thirty takes without success on Mosaic, but Hubbard, Fuller and Shorter played it at a Blakey rehearsal and Blakey finished it.

segments.title: Art Blakey as bandleader: the general, Wayne's 'Those Who Sit and Wait'
segments.summary: Blakey led from behind like a general, kept the band waiting, took one-deal recordings, and showed Walton that intellect did not require a campus; Walton also mentions a San Remo video with his That Old Feeling.

segments.title: Touring Japan with Blakey; Ugetsu, On the Ginza and Orgy in Rhythm
segments.summary: Blakey was a big favorite in Japan, greeting with flowers, which inspired Walton's Ugetsu and Shorter's tunes, and Walton calls those years the prime of his life, plus an Orgy in Rhythm tour.

segments.title: Playing with Blakey: the spaces he left for the pianist
segments.summary: Walton says Blakey played bombastically but left little holes, teaching him to hear when he could be heard.

segments.title: Blakey never read music; his deference to Billy Eckstine
segments.summary: Blakey had no written drum parts, played with Eckstine and acted demure when Walton met Eckstine with him; Walton adds stories of Eckstine's toughness, his knot and his not joining the Rat Pack.

segments.title: Blakey's business side: the stranger who paid the band in Kansas City
segments.summary: Responding to Curtis Fuller's story, Walton recounts Blakey handing out pay through a young woman stranger in Kansas City, his objection, and Jimmy Merritt losing his plane ticket to her.

segments.title: Leaving Blakey for the Five Spot; Lee Morgan, fines for lateness
segments.summary: Tired of traveling, Walton and Reggie Workman left to join a trio at the Five Spot; he adds how Blakey fined him for being late at the Apollo and said the music grew sophisticated with this band.

segments.title: The Blakey sextet: great band, little press coverage
segments.summary: Brower and Walton agree it was one of the finest sextets, yet it never got an article in Downbeat even while working standing-room dates nightly.

segments.title: Blakey's itinerary: European tours and the U.S. club circuit
segments.summary: He lists Europe, Birdland, the Jazz Workshop in San Francisco, Chicago's Jazz Showcase, Minneapolis, Detroit's Minor Key and Cleveland.

segments.title: Audiences and package shows at the Howard Theater
segments.summary: Audiences were mixed, and at Washington's Howard Theater and Baltimore the bill had a comedian MC, singers such as Ray Charles or Betty Carter and often another jazz group.

segments.title: The 1960s as a golden time versus his present
segments.summary: Walton says theater jazz shows peaked while he was with Blakey and a golden era of audiences, but today is golden for him personally as a composer whose pieces others record.

segments.title: The Left Bank Jazz Society and missing the train with Hank Mobley
segments.summary: Walton remembers the Baltimore Left Bank Jazz Society and arriving late with Hank Mobley after nearly boarding the one train from Penn Station.

segments.title: Left Bank dates with Gene Ammons, Sonny Stitt and Lucky Thompson
segments.summary: Walton compares the contrasting personalities of Sonny Stitt, who competed, and Gene Ammons, who refused, and Lucky Thompson, who resented the contest after Ammons died.

segments.title: Etta Jones live at the Left Bank and Joel Dorn's unpaid musicians
segments.summary: Walton's trio with Sam Jones and Billy Higgins backed Etta Jones on a live tape later issued by Joel Dorn, whom Walton says never followed through on paying the families.

segments.title: Mingus's tantrum at the Five Spot and Abbey Lincoln's trio request
segments.summary: While Walton's trio played opposite Mingus, Mingus wrecked his bass in a fit, and Abbey Lincoln told Max Roach this was the trio she wanted to record with.

segments.title: Wayne Shorter leaves Blakey for Miles; Weather Report and Zawinul
segments.summary: Walton recalls Miles slowly courting Shorter, Blakey's doubts about Shorter in Weather Report, and Zawinul admitting to him that he was arrogant.

segments.title: Abbey Lincoln and the Cedar Walton Trio at Wells in Harlem
segments.summary: With Jack DeJohnette newly added, the trio backed Abbey Lincoln for a thirteen-week run at Wells in Harlem until a disco upstairs drowned out the music.

segments.title: Betty Carter replaces Abbey Lincoln and Walton is let go
segments.summary: He recommended Betty Carter to the club; she cut his pay, snapped when he mentioned Abbey, fired him after repeated lateness for John Hicks, and Brower asks about her bassist.

segments.title: Recording 'The Maestro' with Abbey Lincoln
segments.summary: After Sarah Vaughan and Sam Jones passed on his song The Maestro, Abbey Lincoln eagerly recorded it with lyrics by Walton, a rehearsal in L.A., and the group of Bob Berg, Billy Higgins and David Williams.

segments.title: Politics and social content in his music
segments.summary: Asked about Abbey and Max's protest sensibility, Walton says his instrumental music is more like science and not programmatic, except The Maestro, a story about Ellington.

segments.chapter: Piano influences and the Hard Bop label
segments.title: Piano influences: Ellington, Monk, Hank Jones and Bud Powell
segments.summary: He names Ellington's spare piano, Monk, Hank Jones and above all Bud Powell, and laments Powell's illness and treatment.

segments.chapter: Piano influences and the Hard Bop label
segments.title: Thelonious Monk: personal relationship and Walton's take on his music
segments.summary: Monk admired pianists and told Walton to play his own stuff; Walton says he tries to extend what Monk left out.

segments.chapter: Piano influences and the Hard Bop label
segments.title: Art Tatum's influence
segments.summary: Walton listened to Tatum for years, unconsciously emulating but never copying, and notes Tatum's arrangements of standards.

segments.chapter: Piano influences and the Hard Bop label
segments.title: Is Cedar Walton a Romantic? Love of ballads and standards
segments.summary: Brower suggests a romantic affection for standards; Walton does not know the term but admits he loves love songs and has heard hundreds of songs he recreates in his style.

segments.chapter: Piano influences and the Hard Bop label
segments.title: Hank Jones, perfectionist and gentleman
segments.summary: Walton knows Hank Jones only minimally, from Japan tours and his dry humor, and describes him rehearsing Carmen McRae's music in a practice room.

segments.chapter: Piano influences and the Hard Bop label
segments.title: End of Day One
segments.summary: Staff discuss the remaining time and Walton agrees to continue tomorrow.

segments.chapter: Piano influences and the Hard Bop label
segments.title: Day Two opens: the 'Hard Bop' label versus bebop
segments.summary: Brower opens Day Two at the Dupont Hotel asking about being called a Hard Bop pianist; Walton calls it a journalists' term and says it is simply bebop, and praises Ellington's interludes.

segments.chapter: Piano influences and the Hard Bop label
segments.title: Billy Strayhorn and Ellington: alter-ego, hidden talent, Satin Doll
segments.summary: Walton calls Strayhorn Ellington's alter-ego, says being Black and gay kept Strayhorn from being presented in the 1940s, and was surprised to learn Strayhorn wrote Satin Doll.

segments.chapter: Piano influences and the Hard Bop label
segments.title: Hard Bop again: Horace Silver and Monk as composer-leaders
segments.summary: Pressed on gospel and groove traits, Walton accepts the label only as journalism and points to Horace Silver and Monk, who featured mostly their own compositions.

segments.chapter: Piano influences and the Hard Bop label
segments.title: Walton's Monk medley, stride piano and the Romantic question
segments.summary: He plays a Monk medley, calls Monk self-contained, says stride gave swing-era pianists their base, mentions Ellis Larkins, and revisits whether his ballads are romantic.

segments.title: The Coltrane Giant Steps session and the conversation on the outtake
segments.summary: Walton explains that he first recorded Giant Steps material with Coltrane, Paul Chambers and Lex Humphries before the replacements, that Javon Jackson found their outtake chat, and that he declined a solo.

segments.title: Coltrane as neighbor: constant practicing and the Berlin intermission story
segments.summary: Walton and Lex Humphries visited Coltrane near his apartment, hearing him play around the clock; at a club with three bands Betty Carter asked Walton to stop Coltrane practicing and he could not.

segments.title: The jazz-corner club with three bands: Basie, Betty Carter, Blakey and Trane
segments.summary: Walton describes the basement club's layout and capacity, hearing Basie and Joe Williams for the first time on a bill with Betty Carter, Blakey and Coltrane, and Brower asks about the economics.

segments.title: Set lengths and playing opposite Coltrane at Alice Tully Hall
segments.summary: Walton describes how evenings might unfold, an hour sets, and hearing Trane's quartet over the PA from the bar at the old Lincoln Center before Blakey played.

segments.title: Coltrane's changing direction in the mid-1960s
segments.summary: Brower asks whether people debated where Coltrane was going; Walton says not then, praises Elvin and McCoy as perfect fits, and admits he was focused on his own career with Blakey.

segments.title: Ornette Coleman, Don Cherry and Billy Higgins at the Five Spot
segments.summary: Walton went to the Five Spot whenever he returned from the road in 1959-60, was blown away by Ornette's quartet, and enjoyed it as a fan rather than seeing controversy.

segments.title: Cecil Taylor and sharing David Amram's piano
segments.summary: Walton says no avant-garde player annoyed him, and recalls he and Cecil Taylor each had keys to David Amram's apartment to practice, leaving them mutual admirers.

segments.title: David Amram and a women's college gig with Sonny Rollins
segments.summary: Walton and Brower talk about David Amram's character, and Walton recalls a Sunday gig with Rollins at a women's college where Rollins squatted to talk with students after returning from Chicago.

segments.title: Walton's dry wit on the bandstand: 'young and foolish', dyeing his hair
segments.summary: Brower asks about Walton's humor; he says his stage patter is just natural and does not enter his playing except titles, with a Dallas joke that drew silence and a Tex Ritter line on hair.

segments.title: Quotations and repartee on the bandstand
segments.summary: They discuss musicians quoting songs and answering each other as a quick private wit; Walton says it is for themselves, unplanned, and the audience can't tell a laugh at a mistake.

segments.title: David Williams: how he came to the trio and his Trinidad music
segments.summary: Sam Jones sent David Williams to Boomers, where he offered to start the set; Walton praises his beat and describes his Trinidadian pan music with little market.

segments.title: David Williams's family names: Mary Lou, Noble Sissle and a bass-playing father
segments.summary: Walton and Brower talk about Williams's Trinidadian accent, his bassist father John Buddy and siblings named for Mary Lou Williams and Noble Sissle, with an aside about the Sissle and Blake book.

segments.title: Sam Jones's beat, David Williams, and Peterson's big dinners
segments.summary: The trio was Billy Higgins and Sam Jones, then David Williams after Sam's death on Sam's recommendation; Walton prizes Jones's impeccable beat and his time with Cannonball, Monk and Oscar Peterson. Walton wants beat and harmony from a bassist, and says Sam Jones tired of Peterson's tours and enormous dinners, as Alvin Queen later told him.

segments.title: Billy Higgins: the instant-fire drummer for a trio
segments.summary: Walton says Higgins was on fire from the downbeat with no buildup, the ideal trio drummer, with Willie Jones sharing the trait.

segments.title: Blakey's delicate trio drumming versus his sextet power
segments.summary: Brower contrasts loud drummers with cymbal-detail players; Walton says Blakey adjusted for trio work, as on Monk records.

segments.title: Playing Stevie Wonder and Beatles pieces
segments.summary: Walton recorded Stevie Wonder pieces like My Cherie Amour and Another Star, found them irresistible in his forties or fifties, and says borrowing from other genres is common in jazz.

segments.title: His listening habits and Jonathan Schwartz's radio show
segments.summary: Walton listens to Jonathan Schwartz's PBS radio program and recently met Schwartz at an event for singer Hilary Kole.

segments.title: Doing his own bookings; Europe dates and the Beirut engagement
segments.summary: Walton enjoys booking himself without commissions, details upcoming Helsinki, Hamburg, London and Beirut dates, and Brower jokes about not wanting to go to Beirut.

segments.title: Live performance over recording; streaming and taxes
segments.summary: Walton says he plays live more than he records for HighNote, expects streaming to replace CDs, and does his own payroll taxes with an accountant Javon Jackson recommended.

segments.title: Publishing: Harry Fox, BMI, his own company and business advice
segments.summary: He explains Harry Fox, BMI and his own publishing company that gives an annual guarantee, and says Benny Golson and Gigi Gryce advised him that in jazz publishing just means ownership.

segments.title: How big is his body of compositions
segments.summary: Walton estimates around two hundred recorded compositions, notes his catalog took a full page in the Playboy Jazz Festival program.

segments.title: Recognition as a composer; how he writes and naming Mosaic
segments.summary: Walton says recognition is others recording his work, with Bolivia the most recorded, describes writing from the piano or a title like Mosaic on a billboard, and says he has composed since age six or seven.

segments.title: Why he will never retire
segments.summary: Walton says playing for people is the best thing that could happen to an artist and compares himself to Ahmad Jamal who always says he is retiring.

segments.chapter: NEA Jazz Master, family and the future
segments.title: NEA Jazz Master ceremony: Dear Ruth with the Lincoln Center orchestra
segments.summary: Walton was proud to be named a 2010 NEA Jazz Master, played his piece Dear Ruth for his mother with the Lincoln Center Jazz Orchestra, and recalls other honorees including Muhal Richard Abrams.

segments.chapter: NEA Jazz Master, family and the future
segments.title: Walton's children: Carl, Rodney, Cedra and Nyesha
segments.summary: He introduces his children from his first marriage in the 1960s, their names and careers, and says he raised the family as a sideman and jazz musician.

segments.chapter: NEA Jazz Master, family and the future
segments.title: Estate planning and the John Hicks family dispute
segments.summary: Asked about his catalog's future income, Walton says a will is in progress with his current wife's cousin, citing the bickering over John Hicks's estate.

segments.chapter: NEA Jazz Master, family and the future
segments.title: Orchestrating for large ensembles: Faddis's orchestra and Nicholas Payton
segments.summary: Walton prefers small groups and only orchestrated Dear Ruth for John Faddis's orchestra, which also played arrangements by Frank Foster and Rufus Reid, and he and Brower try to recall a New Orleans trumpeter's name, Nicholas Payton.

segments.chapter: NEA Jazz Master, family and the future
segments.title: Banter: an album called 'Wow', big-band money and Blakey's Brinks truck
segments.summary: Brower proposes a big-band album titled Wow and software orchestration; Walton jokes there is no big money in this art, quoting Blakey that no Brinks truck follows a hearse.

segments.chapter: NEA Jazz Master, family and the future
segments.title: Looking ahead: the Beirut engagement and missing bombings by a day
segments.summary: Walton says he is thrilled to be asked to Beirut for solo sets, jokes about narrowly missing bombings in Israel, and Brower admits he is skittish.

segments.chapter: NEA Jazz Master, family and the future
segments.title: Jazz Masters group with Bobby Hutcherson and the Timeless All Stars
segments.summary: Walton describes a Hutcherson-Walton group with David Williams and Eddie Marshall that toured, then mentions Timeless All Stars with Harold Land, Higgins and Curtis Fuller.

segments.chapter: NEA Jazz Master, family and the future
segments.title: Parting shots: advice to students to choose a path and stay on it
segments.summary: Asked for closing words, Walton tells young musicians to keep striving for excellence and stay on one path, and jokes about playing D.C. versus Beirut.

segments.chapter: NEA Jazz Master, family and the future
segments.title: Closing thanks to the Smithsonian and end of interview
segments.summary: Walton thanks Brower and Kimery and the Smithsonian archive, jokes about faxes and Jazz Masters funders, and says the interview sets the record straight.
